lessons.title: Animal health for small-scale livestock farmers
lessons.html:
Serving small-scale farmers

This three-year Diploma in Animal Health (NQF 6) balances theory with practical training and is aimed especially at supporting small-scale and emerging livestock farmers. These farmers keep a few cattle, goats, sheep, pigs or chickens, often on communal land or small plots, and their animals are central to household income and food security.

Understanding the farmer's situation

  • Limited cash for medicines and vaccines, so advice must be affordable.
  • Long distances to vets and co-ops.
  • Shared grazing and water with neighbours' animals, so disease spreads easily.
  • Few handling facilities: often no crush, so animals are caught in the kraal.
  • Strong local knowledge that should be respected and built on.

Priority health problems

SpeciesCommon problems
CattleTicks and tick-borne diseases, lumpy skin disease, poor winter nutrition, calf losses
Goats and sheepWire-worm, pneumonia, heartwater, abortions
PigsAfrican swine fever, mange, worms
Village chickensNewcastle disease, external parasites, predators

Affordable prevention

Prevention costs far less than treating sick animals or losing them. Practical steps include vaccinating chickens against Newcastle disease, keeping pigs penned and never feeding them uncooked kitchen waste (a risk for African swine fever), regular dipping at the community dip tank, deworming goats only when FAMACHA scores show anaemia, and building up winter feed such as hay or crop residues.

lessons.title: Practical skills and working with communities
lessons.html:
Hands-on skills

Practical training is a large part of this diploma. Students practise on farms, at state veterinary offices and at clinics so that they can do the job confidently. Core skills include:

  • Safe catching and restraint of cattle, small stock, pigs and poultry, even without a crush.
  • Clinical examination: temperature, heart and breathing rate, mucous membrane colour, body condition.
  • Giving injections under the skin and into the muscle at the right site, and oral dosing with a drench gun.
  • Collecting blood, faeces and skin scrapings for the laboratory.
  • Assisting at births, treating simple wounds and navel infections.
  • Keeping treatment and vaccination records.

Safety when restraining animals

Work with at least one helper, keep calm and quiet, and plan an escape route before entering a kraal with cattle. Never stand directly behind cattle, and never wrap a rope around your hand. Use a halter and tie with a quick-release knot. Pigs can bite, so use a pig board or snare as trained.

Working with the community

The best technicians build trust. They arrive when promised, explain what they are doing and why, and involve local leaders and livestock associations. Training a few community animal health workers to vaccinate chickens or recognise disease extends the reach of the service. Farmers' days at the dip tank, demonstrations and simple printed guides in local languages all help.

Linking farmers to markets

Healthy animals earn more. Technicians can explain how auction buyers judge condition, why animals must be branded or tattooed under the Animal Identification Act 6 of 2002, and why withdrawal periods must be observed before selling (follow the product label or the vet).

Key points

  • Small-scale farmers need affordable, practical animal health advice.
  • Prevention, such as Newcastle vaccination and not feeding raw swill to pigs, saves money.
  • Core practical skills include restraint, clinical examination, injections and sampling.
  • Restrain animals safely: helpers, escape routes, quick-release knots.
  • Build trust with communities and link healthy animals to markets.
